title: Russia Burns Through Gold at Fastest Pace Since 1998 as Indonesia Faces MSCI Ejection
subhead: Russia's central bank sold 62 tonnes of gold in 10 months to fund a widening war deficit, Indonesia held rates amid a shock MSCI downgrade threat, and France's 10-year yield breached 5% for the first time since 2002.

sections.heading: Russia's Gold Reserves Drop to Lowest Since 2019 as War Deficit Widens
sections.body:
Russia's central bank sold gold from its reserves for a 10th consecutive month in September, reducing holdings by 6.2 metric tonnes to 72.8 million troy ounces — the lowest level since late 2019, according to central bank figures released Tuesday and reported by The Moscow Times and Kitco.

The bank has drawn down approximately 62 tonnes (2 million ounces) since December, marking the largest sustained sell-off since the 1998 financial crisis, when Russia defaulted on domestic debt and the ruble collapsed. IMF data confirms that only the 1998 drawdown was larger in modern Russian history.

The sales are linked to central bank operations that mirror earlier transactions by the Finance Ministry involving the National Wealth Fund, Russia's rainy-day fund. The budget deficit is expected to reach 7.3 trillion rubles this year, twice the original target, as falling oil and gas revenue increases reliance on reserve assets. Alexander Potavin, an analyst at Finam, told The Moscow Times that high global gold prices had likely encouraged the central bank to step up sales.

Separately, Russian gold exports to China have risen sharply. About 100 tonnes of Russian-origin gold entered Hong Kong between January and July, three times the volume recorded in the same period a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. Russian suppliers have redirected exports eastward since losing access to London, the world's largest gold trading hub.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia is liquidating its hard-asset reserves to finance a war budget that oil and gas revenue can no longer cover. The speed of the drawdown — the fastest since the 1998 default — signals fiscal stress that sanctions and reduced energy income have made structural. The pivot of gold flows toward China also reveals the emerging financial corridor bypassing Western markets.

sections.heading: Indonesia Holds Rates as MSCI Expulsion Threat Triggers Market Rout
sections.body:
Bank Indonesia left its policy rate unchanged at 5.75% for a fourth straight meeting on Wednesday, even as the rupiah weakened following MSCI's surprise downgrade consultation. The Deposit Facility rate was raised to 5.00% from 4.75%, a partial tightening move.

MSCI announced last week a consultation on reclassifying Indonesia's stock index from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status, bypassing the Frontier Market tier altogether. A final decision is expected by June 2027. Reuters reported that the move could cut Indonesia off from global capital flows, and the Jakarta Composite Index has sold off sharply since the announcement.

The Indonesia Stock Exchange moved to exclude high-concentration stocks from the JCI after a meeting with MSCI, Tempo.co reported. Bloomberg reported that rate-hike bets have jumped as the MSCI threat pressures the rupiah, while Brown Brothers Harriman noted that BI projects the current account deficit to widen to between 1.6% and 2.4% of GDP in 2026, raising external funding needs precisely as MSCI downgrade risks threaten capital outflows.

BI's $125 billion in FX reserves (8.4% of GDP) provide a buffer, but the central bank faces a narrowing path: hold rates to support growth and risk capital flight, or hike to defend the currency and dampen domestic demand.
sections.whyItMatters: An MSCI ejection would remove Indonesia from the portfolios of passive emerging-market funds worldwide, potentially triggering billions in forced outflows. The episode exposes how index inclusion has become a pillar of emerging-market financial stability — and how fragile that pillar can be when governance and free-float concerns collide with institutional capital.

sections.heading: French 10-Year Yield Breaches 5% for First Time Since 2002
sections.body:
France's 10-year bond yield surpassed 5% on Wednesday for the first time since 2002, as reported by CNBC, Le Monde, and The Guardian. French borrowing costs have hit a 24-year high amid a combination of civil unrest, budget fears, and widening spreads against German bunds.

The French OAT spread over German bunds reached approximately 153 basis points, according to TradingNEWS data cited on Tuesday. The yield surge reflects investor concern over France's fiscal trajectory and political instability, with widespread protests compounding market anxiety.

The bond turmoil is complicating the ECB's rate decision ahead of next week's policy meeting. ECB Governing Council member Madis Kazaks said Wednesday that more policy tightening may be necessary if inflation continues to reside above target, though he noted that the recent rise in yields has already tightened financing conditions, Bloomberg's Econostream reported. Separately, ECB Chief Economist Philip Lane said greater global euro use could help the ECB control inflation, and the ECB published analysis suggesting that AI and reduced fossil-fuel dependence are helping the eurozone weather the energy shock.

ECB's Joachim Nagel called for Europe to deepen its banking and capital markets integration, while the Bundesbank noted that the German economy likely stagnated in Q3 with a modest recovery expected in Q4.
sections.whyItMatters: France at 5% is a stark signal that political dysfunction and fiscal slippage are being priced into sovereign debt in real time. With the ECB meeting next week and at least one Governing Council member openly discussing further tightening, the clash between market-driven tightening and political crisis in the eurozone's second-largest economy is becoming the central tension in European monetary policy.

sections.heading: OPEC+ Holds November Output Steady, Cuts Demand Forecast Again
sections.body:
OPEC+ agreed to keep November oil output targets unchanged, EnergyNow.com and ThisDayLive reported on Wednesday. The decision comes despite Brent crude trading above $108 after briefly topping $110, with Hormuz shipping risks persisting amid the ongoing Iran conflict.

OPEC further lowered its 2026 global oil demand growth forecast, the second consecutive cut, citing economic headwinds. The cartel said oil supplies are adequate and blamed war fears for elevated prices, Petroleum News reported.

Bank forecasts diverged sharply. Citi raised its Brent forecast and sees $150 oil if Hormuz disruption persists. Goldman Sachs lowered its forecasts, seeing Brent falling to $90 while warning of $125 in 2027. JP Morgan sees Brent staying in the low $100s even if Hormuz reopens by June. UBS cut its forecasts on improved Hormuz oil flows, while HSBC's chief said Hormuz could become redundant in five years.

A Reuters perspective by EnergyNow's Ron Bousso argued that the UAE's exit from OPEC strips the cartel of clout and risks a bitter price war, particularly if Hormuz reopens and suppressed supply floods the market. OPEC+ agreed to boost output once Hormuz reopens, but that deal is described as 'irrelevant for now' by Reuters analyst Clyde Russell, given that the strait remains shut.
sections.whyItMatters: OPEC+ is frozen: it cannot raise output while Hormuz is blocked, and the demand outlook is softening. The real story is the divergence in bank forecasts — a $60 spread between Citi's $150 and Goldman's $90 — which reveals that the market is pricing political outcomes, not supply fundamentals. When Hormuz reopens, the output hike agreement could trigger a price collapse if demand hasn't recovered.

sections.heading: First Lawsuit Filed Against Trump's Section 338 Tariffs on Canada
sections.body:
The Liberty Justice Center filed the first lawsuit challenging Trump's Section 338 tariffs on Canadian imports on Tuesday, representing a New Jersey food importer. The suit, filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade, argues that the 50% tariffs on Canadian goods illegally rely on a 1930 statute that was superseded by subsequent trade law, Reuters, CNBC, BBC, and The New York Times reported.

The lawsuit argues that Section 338's 'launch requirements' — conditions that must be met before the tariff authority can be invoked — were not satisfied. The plaintiffs contend that the statute cannot be used because Congress has since enacted comprehensive trade regimes, including the Trade Act of 1974 and the USMCA, that supersede the 1930 provision.

The legal challenge follows Canada's announcement of an $8.7 billion partnership between the federal government and Ontario to support steel, auto, and critical mineral sectors hit by the tariff war. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled the plan on Wednesday, with Carney saying Trump's tariffs hurt Americans and CBC reporting that hopes for a U.S. trade deal are fading.

Bloomberg reported that U.S.-Mexico trade talks have hit an impasse as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick exerts influence over the negotiations. Mexico is seeking tariff relief on aluminum, steel, and vehicles before year-end, according to Mexico News Daily.
sections.whyItMatters: The Section 338 lawsuit is the first legal test of a tariff authority that has never been used in modern history. If the court strikes it down, the entire Canada tariff regime collapses. If it upheld, it validates a sweeping executive tariff power that bypasses Congress. The $8.7 billion Canadian support package signals that Ottawa is settling in for a prolonged trade conflict rather than betting on a negotiated resolution.

sections.heading: Ukraine's Anti-Corruption Bureau Searches Central Bank Governor's Premises
sections.body:
Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) searched the premises of Andriy Pyshnyi, head of the National Bank of Ukraine, on October 21, the Kyiv Independent reported. NABU said in a statement that it is 'conducting searches at the National Bank of Ukraine and at the home of one of its employees,' with no one detained or charged.

The central bank confirmed the reports and said it 'continues to operate as usual.' Media reports, including by TodayPress.tv and UkrMedia, speculated that Pyshnyi had submitted his resignation, though the National Bank denied rumors about his departure, according to UNN. The New Voice of Ukraine reported that speculation is growing over his possible resignation.

The searches are reportedly linked to the central bank's failure to prevent a HR 150 million ($3.4 million) payment through state-owned Sense Bank allegedly funded with laundered money and posted as bail for former Energy and Justice Minister Herman Halushchenko in June. The central bank has faced criticism for not addressing alleged criminal schemes involving Sense Bank more broadly.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's central bank is a key institution in managing IMF disbursements, sovereign debt restructuring, and wartime financial stability. A corruption investigation targeting its governor — regardless of outcome — risks undermining confidence in the institution at a time when Ukraine's financial credibility with Western donors and the IMF is under intense scrutiny.

bottomLine: Three stories defined the day: Russia is burning through gold reserves at a pace not seen since its 1998 default to fund a war deficit twice the original target, exposing the fiscal toll of sanctions and reduced energy revenue. Indonesia faces a potential MSCI ejection that could sever it from global capital flows, and its central bank chose a partial tightening compromise that satisfies neither growth nor currency defense. France's 10-year yield at 5% — a 24-year high — with ECB policymakers split on further tightening, puts the eurozone's political-fiscal tension directly into next week's rate decision. Meanwhile, OPEC+ is paralyzed by the Hormuz shutdown with bank forecasts diverging by $60, and the first legal challenge to Trump's Canada tariffs begins a court process that could invalidate the entire Section 338 tariff regime.
